title: Jamey Aebersold camps and letting students create
summary: Everyone can improvise; he taught for Aebersold and at Skidmore.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. So you did some work with the Jamey Aebersold camps, so I want to know, like Jamey says, can anyone improvise?

Well I think they can. I was talking about that — I watched a beautiful documentary this morning called “Moonlight Sonata” and it was all about a deaf child who got cochlear implants when he was young, and he got to hear, and he ended up performing. And it was a beautiful documentary. And I was telling my wife, I said, you know I used to do that with my classical players, and I said Jamey used to do that too. Even though you’re working on a certain performance piece in a lesson, you should always let the student at some point in the lesson make up something of their own so they get the feeling of creating something. Even if it sounds horrible. And that’s why Jamey puts on those one- chord Dorian vamps and just says, “play something.” You know just play a couple of notes, what do you hear? He just tries to get them to come out of that just reading situation. I taught for Jamey for many years and then I moved on to the Skidmore Institute you know, in Albany, New York, in Saratoga. At Skidmore College they have a summer institute there. I worked there with Milt Hinton and Eddie Shaughnessy and so many guys. But I just ended up being a teacher, which is something I never thought I’d go into.
